issues.legal_issue: A transfer of immovable property in India by a person who is not an Indian citizen, made without the required prior permission, is unenforceable until permission is granted.
material_facts: A foreign owner gifted part of immovable property in India without obtaining prior permission from the Reserve Bank of India.
No permission was obtained for the gifts, which were challenged in a civil suit by a person claiming title under a separately approved sale of the larger property.
issues.conclusion: The prior-permission requirement was mandatory. The gifts were unenforceable and not binding until permission was granted; the suit was decreed, including relief for possession and mesne profits subject to a separate inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 required prior permission for the specified transfers by non-citizens. Read with Sections 47, 50 and 63, its purpose and scheme make the requirement mandatory, and a prohibited agreement cannot be enforced under Sections 10 and 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The Court applied Mannalal Khetan v. Kedar Nath Khetan, which explains that a statutory penalty may imply prohibition and render a prohibited transaction unenforceable; it also considered Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd., Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. and Vijay Karia v. Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi SRL. The Court clarified that such a transaction need not be a nullity, but is unenforceable until permission is granted.

rule.if: civil_challenge_to_property_transfer and foreign_transferor and immovable_property_in_india and no_prior_permission

predicates.civil_challenge_to_property_transfer: A civil proceeding challenged the enforceability of a transfer of property.
predicates.foreign_transferor: A person who was not an Indian citizen made the transfer.
predicates.immovable_property_in_india: The transferred property was immovable property situated in India.
predicates.no_prior_permission: The transferor had not obtained the required general or special permission before making the transfer.

issues.definition: When a civil challenge concerns an Indian immovable-property transfer by a non-citizen made without prior permission, the transfer is unenforceable until permission is granted.

issues.legal_issue: A person directly or indirectly affected by an unauthorised property transfer may challenge its enforceability in direct or collateral proceedings.
material_facts: A claimant who asserted an interest in the property challenged gifts made by a foreign owner without prior permission.
The challenge was brought in a civil suit concerning title to and possession of the property.
issues.conclusion: A person directly or indirectly affected by such a transfer may challenge it, whether by direct action or by collateral or indirect challenge.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the mandatory prior-permission requirement under Section 31 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 may be invoked by anyone directly or indirectly affected by the transaction. It relied on the distinction between direct and collateral challenges discussed in Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University and the public-policy and statutory-prohibition principles applied in Mannalal Khetan v. Kedar Nath Khetan.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_transfer_validity: A proceeding sought to challenge the validity or enforceability of a property transfer.
predicates.foreign_transfer_without_prior_permissio: A non-citizen transferred Indian immovable property without the required prior permission.
predicates.claimant_directly_or_indirectly_affected: The claimant was directly or indirectly affected by the transfer.

issues.definition: A claimant affected directly or indirectly by a non-citizen’s unauthorised transfer may challenge its validity or enforceability in the proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: Permission required before a property transfer cannot be replaced by permission obtained after the transfer.
material_facts: The gifts were executed before any permission was obtained.
No permission was subsequently obtained for those gifts.
issues.conclusion: The required permission had to be obtained before the transfer took effect; ex post facto permission was not available for a transfer governed by the prior-permission requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 expressly required previous permission. The Court distinguished Section 31 from Section 29, as discussed in Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd.: Section 29 did not use the same requirement of prior permission and could permit ex post facto approval, whereas Section 31 could not.

predicates.transaction_requires_advance_permission: The applicable legal regime requires permission to be obtained before the transaction takes effect.
predicates.transfer_occurred_before_permission: The transfer took effect before the required permission was obtained.

issues.definition: If a transaction requires advance permission and the transfer occurs first, later permission cannot validate it.

issues.legal_issue: The Court's prospective overruling of contrary decisions does not reopen transactions that had already become final through a competent court's decision.
material_facts: High Courts had issued conflicting decisions on whether transfers made without prior permission were enforceable.
The governing legislation had been repealed, and the Court noted a subsequent shift in policy concerning foreign investment.
The Court considered the need to address existing transactions that had already become final, including through decisions of competent courts.
issues.conclusion: The contrary High Court decisions were overruled prospectively, and transactions already final, including those made final by a competent court, were not to be reopened or disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Exercising its plenary power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, the Court directed prospective overruling in light of the changed investment policy and repeal of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973, while preserving transactions already made final. The Court rejected the argument that there had been a consistent High Court view warranting application of stare decisis, referring to Waman Rao v. Union of India.

predicates.supreme_court_reconsiders_conflicting_pr: The Supreme Court reconsidered conflicting prior decisions on a legal issue.
predicates.contrary_decisions_overruled_prospective: The Supreme Court directed that contrary decisions would be overruled only prospectively.
predicates.transaction_already_final: The transaction had already become final, including through a decision of a competent court.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court prospectively overrules conflicting decisions, a transaction already final is not reopened.
